contact_edits.before: I have few complaints, though, about the performance. Ruth Madoc-Jones' direction is supple and fluid, the myriad transitions excellently handled with much credit to Kimberly Purtell's bare set and bold, sensitive lighting. Of the players, Dawson herself is better at timing her lines than exploring what's beneath them; it's unfortunate, too, that she has to make much of the running in the first quarter of the evening. (I doubt if it was meant to be The Tracy Dawson Show, but it does come on that way.) Powell does unobtrusively and resourcefully well, especially with the night's first monologue. Healey explores, endearingly, many shades of rumpled; at one point he had me convinced that he'd changed the colour of his hair, though all he'd really done was muss it up a little. Dodd shows off the greatest range, from rage to loss to (occasional) glee, and hits each unfussily on the nose; I've never thought of her as a revue performer, and I doubt if she has either, but she has the economy and versatility for it. Some of the scenes -- I almost said numbers -- do echo or complete others, but this doesn't add up to structure. It's as if a Second City running gag were being asked, single-handedly, to repeal the law of diminishing returns - Them And Us Runs until Jan. 31. Call 416-504-7529 for more information.
